setup_steps.title: Try SQL in your browser
setup_steps.body: Open SQLBolt. Each lesson has a small table and a box where you type SQL and see the result straight away, with nothing to install.

setup_steps.title: Install DB Browser for SQLite
setup_steps.body: When you're ready to make your own tables, download DB Browser for SQLite and install it. It's free and works on Windows, Mac and Linux.

setup_steps.title: Make your first database
setup_steps.body: In DB Browser, click New Database and save it as practice.db. Open the Execute SQL tab, type SELECT 1 + 1; and press the play button. If you see 2, you're set up.

project_ideas.title: An org's member list
project_ideas.brief: Make two tables, members and events, fill them with a few rows, and write queries that answer real questions: who joined this year, who attended each event, and how many came.
done_when: Both tables exist and have at least five rows each.
One query filters members with WHERE.
One query joins members to events.
One query counts attendees with GROUP BY.

topics.title: Reading data with SELECT
topics.summary: Get rows and columns out of a table with SELECT and FROM.
topics.why_it_matters: Almost every app keeps its data in tables. SELECT is how you read it, and it's the first thing anyone writes in SQL.

key_terms.definition: Data in rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
One record in a table, like one student.
Chooses which columns to get back.

topics.explanation:
A database keeps data in tables. Each table has columns, like name and course, and rows, one for each record.

A query asks the database a question. SELECT says which columns you want, and FROM says which table they come from. SELECT name, course FROM students; gives every student's name and course.

Use * to get every column. End each query with a semicolon. SQL keywords aren't case-sensitive, but writing them in capitals makes queries easier to read.
topics.example:
-- The students table:
-- id | name  | course | year
--  1 | Ana   | BSCS   | 2
--  2 | Ben   | BSIT   | 1
--  3 | Carla | BSCS   | 3

SELECT name, course FROM students;
topics.example_output:
name  | course
Ana   | BSCS
Ben   | BSIT
Carla | BSCS
tips: Spell column names exactly as they are in the table, or you'll get a "no such column" error.
SELECT * is handy for looking around, but name the columns you need in real queries.

skill_questions.prompt: Which query gets every column of the books table?
In a table, what is one record called?

quiz_items.prompt: Choose columns: ___ name FROM students;
quiz_items.explanation: SELECT lists the columns you want back.

quiz_items.prompt: Say which table: SELECT name ___ students;
quiz_items.hint: Where does the data come from?
quiz_items.explanation: FROM names the table the columns come from.

quiz_items.prompt: Get every column: SELECT ___ FROM students;
quiz_items.explanation: * stands for all columns.

quiz_items.prompt: End a query with a ___
quiz_items.explanation: The semicolon marks where one query ends, so you can write several in a row.

topics.title: Filtering with WHERE
topics.summary: Keep only the rows you need with WHERE, AND, OR and LIKE.
topics.why_it_matters: Tables can have thousands of rows, and you rarely want them all. WHERE asks for just the ones that match.

key_terms.definition: Keeps only the rows where a condition is true.
Join two conditions: both must be true, or either one.
Matches text against a pattern, with % for any characters.

topics.explanation:
WHERE comes after FROM and holds a condition. Only rows where the condition is true come back.

Compare with =, <> (not equal), <, >, <= and >=. Text goes in single quotes, like course = 'BSCS'. Join conditions with AND when both must be true, or OR when either is enough.

LIKE matches patterns in text. % stands for any number of characters, so name LIKE 'A%' finds names that start with A.
topics.example:
-- The students table:
-- id | name  | course | year
--  1 | Ana   | BSCS   | 2
--  2 | Ben   | BSIT   | 1
--  3 | Carla | BSCS   | 3

SELECT name, year
FROM students
WHERE course = 'BSCS' AND year >= 2;
tips: Put text in single quotes: 'BSCS'. Without them, SQL thinks it's a column name.
In SQL, = compares; there's no == like in other languages.

skill_questions.code_snippet:
SELECT name FROM students
WHERE year = 1;

skill_questions.prompt: Which pattern finds names ending in "a"?

quiz_items.prompt: Keep only matching rows: SELECT * FROM students ___ year = 3;
quiz_items.explanation: WHERE filters the rows, keeping only those where the condition is true.

quiz_items.prompt: Both must be true: WHERE year = 2 ___ course = 'BSIT'
quiz_items.explanation: AND keeps a row only when both conditions are true.

quiz_items.prompt: Match a pattern: WHERE name ___ 'J%'
quiz_items.explanation: LIKE compares text to a pattern; % matches any characters.

quiz_items.prompt: In a LIKE pattern, any number of characters is written as ___
quiz_items.explanation: % matches zero or more characters, so 'A%' means anything that starts with A.

topics.title: Sorting and limiting
topics.summary: Put results in order with ORDER BY, and keep the top few with LIMIT.
topics.why_it_matters: Leaderboards, newest posts first, the five cheapest items: most lists people see are sorted and cut short.

key_terms.definition: Sorts the results by one or more columns.
Returns at most a set number of rows.

topics.explanation:
Without ORDER BY, rows come back in whatever order the database likes. ORDER BY column sorts them, lowest first, or A to Z for text.

Add DESC after the column to sort highest first. ASC means lowest first and is the default, so you rarely need to write it.

LIMIT goes at the very end and caps how many rows come back. Together, ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 3 gives the top three.
topics.example:
-- The scores table:
-- name  | score
-- Ana   | 88
-- Ben   | 95
-- Carla | 79
-- Dan   | 91

SELECT name, score
FROM scores
ORDER BY score DESC
LIMIT 2;
tips: The order of the parts matters: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, ORDER BY, then LIMIT.
Sort by more than one column with commas: ORDER BY course, name.

skill_questions.prompt: Which query lists products from the cheapest?

quiz_items.prompt: Sort the results: SELECT * FROM books ___ BY title;
quiz_items.explanation: ORDER BY sorts the rows by the column you name.

quiz_items.prompt: Highest first: ORDER BY score ___
quiz_items.explanation: DESC sorts from highest to lowest; the default, ASC, is lowest first.

quiz_items.prompt: Only the first 10 rows: ... ___ 10;
quiz_items.explanation: LIMIT caps how many rows come back and goes at the end of the query.

quiz_items.prompt: LIMIT comes ___ ORDER BY in a query.
quiz_items.explanation: Rows are sorted first, then cut down, so LIMIT is written after ORDER BY.

topics.title: Counting and grouping
topics.summary: Count, add up and average rows with COUNT, SUM and AVG, per group with GROUP BY.
topics.why_it_matters: Reports ask summary questions: how many students per course, the average grade, total sales this month. Aggregates answer them.

key_terms.definition: Works out the average of a column.
Splits rows into groups so each gets its own summary.

topics.explanation:
Aggregate functions turn many rows into one value. COUNT(*) counts rows, SUM(column) adds them up, AVG(column) averages them, and MIN() and MAX() find the smallest and largest.

On its own, an aggregate summarises the whole table. Add GROUP BY column and you get one row per group instead, like one count for each course.

Give a summary column a readable name with AS, like COUNT(*) AS total. To filter groups after counting, use HAVING instead of WHERE.
topics.example:
-- The students table:
-- id | name  | course | year
--  1 | Ana   | BSCS   | 2
--  2 | Ben   | BSIT   | 1
--  3 | Carla | BSCS   | 3

SELECT course, COUNT(*) AS total
FROM students
GROUP BY course;
tips: Every column in SELECT that isn't inside an aggregate should be in GROUP BY.
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups after.

skill_questions.prompt: Which gets the average of the grade column?

quiz_items.prompt: Count the rows: SELECT ___(*) FROM orders;
quiz_items.explanation: COUNT(*) counts every row.

quiz_items.prompt: One result per course: ... ___ BY course;
quiz_items.explanation: GROUP BY makes one group per value, and aggregates are worked out for each group.

quiz_items.prompt: The average price: SELECT ___(price) FROM items;
quiz_items.explanation: AVG() returns the average of a number column.

quiz_items.prompt: Name a result column: SELECT COUNT(*) ___ total FROM students;
quiz_items.explanation: AS gives a column a new name in the results.

topics.title: Joining tables
topics.summary: Combine rows from two tables that share a column, with JOIN and ON.
topics.why_it_matters: Real data is split across tables, like students in one and their enrollments in another. JOIN puts them back together to answer a question.

key_terms.definition: Says which columns must match to pair rows up.
A column that points to a row in another table, like student_id.

topics.explanation:
Databases avoid repeating information. Instead of writing a student's name on every enrollment, the enrollments table keeps a student_id that points to the students table. That pointer is called a foreign key.

JOIN pairs up rows from two tables, and ON says which columns must match: ON students.id = enrollments.student_id.

When both tables have a column with the same name, write table.column so SQL knows which you mean. A plain JOIN (an inner join) keeps only rows that found a match; LEFT JOIN also keeps rows from the first table that have none.
topics.example:
-- students:
-- id | name
--  1 | Ana
--  2 | Ben

-- enrollments:
-- student_id | subject
--  1         | Math
--  1         | Art
--  2         | Math

SELECT students.name, enrollments.subject
FROM students
JOIN enrollments
  ON students.id = enrollments.student_id;
topics.example_output:
name | subject
Ana  | Math
Ana  | Art
Ben  | Math
tips: Forgetting ON pairs every row with every other row. If you get far too many results, check your ON.
Short table names save typing: FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id.

skill_questions.prompt: What does ON do in a JOIN?
Which join also keeps students with no enrollments?

quiz_items.prompt: Combine two tables: FROM students ___ enrollments ON ...
quiz_items.explanation: JOIN combines rows from two tables that match on the ON condition.

quiz_items.prompt: Say how rows match: JOIN enrollments ___ students.id = enrollments.student_id
quiz_items.explanation: ON gives the condition that pairs a row from one table with a row from the other.

quiz_items.prompt: Keep every student, even without a match: ___ JOIN enrollments
quiz_items.hint: The table on the left side stays complete.
quiz_items.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows from the first table and fills missing matches with NULL.

quiz_items.prompt: A column that points to a row in another table is a ___ key.
quiz_items.explanation: A foreign key, like student_id, holds the id of a row in another table.
